transcript:
This message comes from Odu.
Running a business shouldn't feel like surviving a software group project.
Start managing your business with one unified system.
Odu is the all-in-one business management software.
Try for free today at odu.com/nprpodcasts.
Odu delivered a speech at the Warsaw Security Conference in Poland.
Terry Schulz says he's given an overview of how the military alliance would respond if Russia attacked Europe.
There's a lot of concern in Europe about U.S. plans to withdraw troops and military assets.
So U.S. Air Force General Alexis Grinkowicz, and he's NATO's Supreme Allied Commander in Europe,
used this conference to make sure there's no misunderstanding in Moscow that NATO's resolve is weakening.
He unveiled what he called the theory of victory, describing how NATO would use its entire range of capabilities to respond to any attack.
Terry Schulz reporting.
President Trump will fly to Alaska today to campaign for incumbent Republican Senator Dan Sullivan.
Trump's been stumping for GOP candidates, but mostly in states Republicans carry.
After tonight's rally outside Anchorage, Trump will overnight in Las Vegas.
Tomorrow he'll join another rally in Arizona.
An analysis by NPR finds ads promoting the president and his policies continued to be paid for by the U.S. government
well after Trump said his super PAC MAGA Inc. would pick up the tab.
NPR's Tamara Keith reports the administration is now under a court order to take the ads down.
When President Trump announced the U.S. government would no longer be paying for the "patriotic ads,"
about $12 million had already been spent.
But despite giving the impression that there'd been a policy change, the ads didn't stop airing.
In the intervening week, another $10 million in taxpayer dollars went to fund the pro-Trump ads.
That's according to an NPR analysis of ad impact data.
On Sunday, a federal judge issued a temporary order barring future airings.
A White House official not authorized to speak publicly says the last ads paid for by the government aired on Sunday evening.
Tamara Keith, NPR News.
Australia's government says it opposes the Pentagon's plan to livestream the December execution of a former U.S. Army major.
He was convicted of killing 13 people at Fort Hood, Texas in 2009.
Christina Cucaglia reports from Melbourne.
Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese says his government has sought advice on what it can do to block the livestream of the Fort Hood shooter's execution by firing squad.
Speaking to the Australian Broadcasting Corporation, Albanese issued a warning to social media platforms.
I'm making it very clear to them right now that as far as I'm concerned, this has no place in our countries.
Australia's online safety regulator says it doesn't have the power to stop the livestream,
but would monitor if sites are complying with regulations requiring them to protect users from harmful material.
This comes as parliamentarians across the Australian political divide call for the livestream to be banned,
echoing the bipartisan backlash in the U.S.
For NPR News, I'm Christina Cucaglia in Melbourne.
You're listening to NPR News from Washington.
Pope Leo has arrived at a Rome hospital for surgery.
He announced over the weekend that he's having a small, localized nodule removed from one of his lungs.
Leo says he has taken his doctor's advice, and the Vatican says it expects him to take a week to recover.
The amusement park operator Six Flags says it's temporarily closing nine of its roller coasters at a half dozen parks across the U.S.
This follows the death of a person who fell from a coaster yesterday at Six Flags Over Georgia.
That's near Atlanta. From member station WABE, Melissa Fito reports.
Footage from multiple local media outlets shows park staff evacuating riders from the lift hill of Goliath.
The 200-foot hyper coaster opened in 2006.
Cobb County police confirmed several others are injured and the department is investigating the incident.
The Six Flags chain has seen financial challenges and leadership changes since it merged with its once-competitor Cedar Fair in 2024.
This incident comes on the heels of Six Flags Magic Mountain in Southern California,
announcing it's retiring its famous fourth-dimension coaster, X2.
Amid allegations, it has caused several riders serious brain injuries.
For NPR News, I'm Melissa Fito in Atlanta.
More than 60,000 Florida customers are still in the dark after Hurricane Isaias made landfall on the Gulf Coast last Friday.
That's according to the tracking site PowerOutage.us.
Storm killed four people in Florida and Alabama.
I'm Corva Coleman, NPR News in Washington.
